Living under pressure can significantly impact the cognitive abilities of aquanauts — people living underwater for more than a day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Our time on our "space mission" underwater was coming to an end, and I felt like what I imagine an astronaut on the International Space Station (ISS) must feel before returning to Earth. On one hand, you are excited to return to your home and loved ones, as well as to fresh food and normal hygiene. On the other, you know you will miss your crew and the incredible experience of being in space.

While my SEA STAR crew and I had not left Earth during our mission, we were separated from the surface of our home planet for five days. All we saw was a green alien water world surrounding us. We did this to live and work like astronauts on the ISS. Instead of dealing with the challenges of space that astronauts face, we problem-solved sometimes equally difficult issues that divers have to manage when performing research in sea water.

Our "wet ISS" was the Jules' Undersea Lab, which is located near Key Largo, Florida, at 22 feet (7 meters) underwater. By the end of our mission, we had all officially become aquanauts. An aquanaut is an undersea explorer who remains underwater for more than 24 hours, without returning to the surface, in a state known as saturation.

In this sense, saturation refers to the physiological condition achieved by a person who breathes underwater long enough for the body's tissues to absorb the maximum possible amount of inert gas (like nitrogen), for a specific depth and pressure. The term aquanaut derives from the Latin word "aqua" (water) and the Greek "nautes" (sailor).

There were a lot of things I wasn't going to miss about being an aquanaut. They included the constant loud noises our life support systems made to keep us alive underwater, as well as bathroom plumbing issues and some health concerns linked to living under pressure. We also had to be very careful when performing our "spacewalks" (scuba dives), due to the low visibility of the environment around us.

Nonetheless, I experienced a sort of "underview effect" during this mission. Most astronauts report experiencing an "overview effect" after seeing our whole planet from space, which usually makes them value our unique planet even more. I felt a similar thing when I saw the sun's rays come through the water. I couldn't reach them, but I enjoyed them from afar. My everyday life felt so close, yet so far away. It gave me both a feeling of longing and more determination to take even more care of our home world than before.

I'm grateful that we were able to perform all of the different scientific projects we planned for our mission. As the Commander of the crew, I usually have my work cut out for me managing the crew and overseeing their research projects, as had been the case for most of the 40 simulated space missions that I led previously. Fortunately, this time my crew was made up of experienced analog astronauts and divers, so the mission was mostly smooth sailing.

The research we chose for this mission was relevant for long-duration space missions. Since we can only send a small number of astronauts to the ISS with a limited number of research activities to perform, underwater stations provide us with a valuable way to conduct analog, or simulated, space missions instead. We also performed some environmental conservation work using a type of underwater vacuum device to help protect the nature around the Jules' Undersea Lab.

My scientific project was focused on studying whether our cognitive abilities and reaction times changed under pressure. This study is part of my collaboration with the Center for Hyperbaric Medicine, Faculty of Medicine of the University of Ostrava and City Hospital Ostrava in the Czech Republic. The whole crew definitely felt like their response times to these tests were slower during the mission than before it.

We were also interested in seeing how microgreens seeds were affected by the changes in pressure. Our Health & Safety Officer, Dr. Brandy Nunez, grew some of our kale and super salad mix before we started our mission, while other seeds started their growth journey underwater. All seeds were transferred to our underwater station using two varied pressure settings (gradual and sudden pressure release during their descent). After we harvested them, we could see that the latter types of seeds did indeed experience some barotrauma (damage caused by the sudden increase in air pressure).

Executive Officer Paul Bakken's work was related to managing the internal pressure of logistical transfer containers when they are exposed to significant environmental changes in pressure. The fourth crewmember, Mission Specialist Jenn Pint, worked with Interstellar Performance Labs to develop a taxonomy for analyzing environmental and crew interaction factors during simulated space missions.

On top of these projects, we also performed neutral buoyancy experiments during our underwater spacewalks, as well as the testing of environmental sensors developed by high school and university students in Slovakia. The sensors provided important supplemental information to the cognitive study about our simulated space habitat's living conditions.

Just like astronauts on the ISS, we dedicated some of our time to outreach and educational work, too. In our case, we called Cosmic Region, a simulated space station in Slovakia, and gave the team there a tour of our underwater habitat. My crewmembers kindly went into the water at that time and performed a spacewalk to show what our work during the mission was like.

As I put on my "spacesuit" (scuba diving gear) one last time, I breathed the stuffy undersea air once more and then dove out to return to "Earth." My crewmembers and I then took a long detour around the lagoon around us to help our bodies adjust to lower pressures. Even though we were only 22 feet underwater, there was still a small risk of decompression-related problems that aquanauts can face after living under saturation for some time. The final step was to breach the surface at long last. That's when we all enjoyed breathing fresh air again and feeling the sun on our faces, though the temperature in Florida made us quickly hide away from it again 😉.

You can follow Dr. Michaela Musilova at her website and on social media: @astro_michaela (Instagram, TikTok and Threads), @Dr. Michaela Musilova (Facebook) and @astro-michaela.bsky.social (Bluesky).

Dr. Michaela Musilova is an award-winning astrobiologist, explorer, professional speaker and author. Michaela has been conducting space-related research at institutions around the world, including NASA, ESA, CalTech, the Canada-France-Hawaii telescope and many others. She was the Commander of 40 simulated missions to the Moon and Mars — the most missions led to date.

#741. Warner Music Buys Back Part of German Distributor Zebralution, Expanding Reach in Europe

The pioneering digital distributor of music and audiobooks was sold by WMG in 2017 but now returns with enhanced resources.

By Elizabeth Dilts Marshall

Warner Music Group (WMG) said Tuesday (Nov. 3) it had acquired indie record label distributor Zebralution Music GmbH from Bookwire, bringing back part of the Zebralution company it owned for a decade and expanding the major’s reach into the business of serving Germany and Europe.

Zebralution Music is a spinoff of Zebralution Gmbh, which Bookwire acquired from the German performance rights organization GEMA in March 2026. In a press release announcing the Bookwire acquisition at the time, Bookwire described Zebralution as among the first big digital distributors of music, audiobooks, e-books and podcasts, with more than 1,500 label and publisher clients globally. Terms of the deal were not disclosed.

WMG acquired Zebralution in 2007 and sold it in 2017 to its founders Kurt Thielen, Sascha Lazimbat, Christof Ellinghaus and Konrad von Löhneysen. Founded in 2003, Zebralution distributed a catalog of 500,000-plus tracks, albums and videos to hundreds of digital services worldwide at the time WMG sold it.

The reacquisition follows WMG’s April deal to buy B2B music distribution platform Revelator and further expands the reach and services offered through WMG and its distribution and services offerings housed under ADA. Zebralution Music label clients gain access to WMG’s technology, distribution, analytics and financial tools. The company’s now co-CEOs von Löhneysen and Lazimbat will remain with the company “to align strategic operations,” according to a statement.

“This is an exciting new chapter for Zebralution Music, but for our label partners and the people we work with every day, it will very much be business as usual,” Lazimbat said in a statement. “We’ll continue to operate with the same team, the same relationships … What does change is the additional technology and resources now available to us, which will help us build on what we have already achieved.”

Von Löhneysen, whose own label, Embassy of Music, is a Zebralution client, echoed the sentiment that customers should expect “the same people, the same approach and the same independence they’ve always valued.”

Niels Walboomers, president of Warner Music Central Europe, said WMG was drawn to Zebralution’s regional expertise and world-class capabilities.

“Konrad and Sascha have built one of the most trusted homes for independent music in Europe,” Walboomers said.

#740. In ‘Elsinore,’ Billie Piper Found “Beautiful Chaos” With Andrew Scott — And a New Career Chapter

The decorated stage and screen star is a scene-stealer in the weepy Oscar contender, leading to the most attention she's received for a film role to date. The experience is inspiring her to forge a new path.

At the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, just ahead of Halloween weekend, Billie Piper held a masterclass for college students. “It was basically me just rattling on about being an actor — I hope some of it was useful, not sure,” she says the next day from a quiet library in the Southern city’s downtown. “Their line of questioning was so insightful and kind of ahead of their years. They were all there with the little moleskin books taking notes. I just didn’t expect that.”

She’d have little reason to. Despite her decades in the business, despite the Olivier Award win and five BAFTA nominations, the English native hasn’t really traveled the film-festival circuit before. She came to town as an honoree for the Oscar contender Elsinore, receiving the Marquee Award for her vivacious turn as the imperious real-life casting director Patsy Pollock. Related Stories Movies Golden Globes: 'Club Kid' Submitted as Drama (Exclusive) Movies Santa Barbara Film Fest: Inde Navarrette, Jaafar Jackson Among Eight Tapped for Virtuoso Awards

In spending time with the kids before the festivities kicked off, it dawned on her: “I actually thought: ‘God, I’ve done some really great jobs.’”

She arrives today with dark brown hair, a far cry from the striking blonde of Elsinore and her other most noted screen roles, and a tablet that she occasionally flashes open to reference movies she’s either seen recently or intends to soon watch. “It’s really fired me up about independent movies again,” she says of running around in support of Elsinore. (The film launched at Telluride, where star Andrew Scott emerged as an instant best-actor front-runner, and has since played all over the world.) “I felt like it was all dead, but it wasn’t dead. I just feel so jacked about all the movies I’m seeing.”

An intensely chameleonic actress unafraid to go big, Piper has never had the largest footprint in the feature space. “Often the films that I read weren’t that good for women,” she says. We may be at something of a turning point. Already, she’s received her first career British Independent Film Award nomination for Elsinore, competing in a supporting category alongside returning faces like Claire Foy and Tom Courtenay.

After breaking out as a teen pop star, the now-44-year-old has always followed the best work. She made her name onscreen by leading series like Doctor Who and Secret Diary of a Callgirl, then as a major stage actor in West End productions of The Effect and Yerma. For the latter revival of Federico García Lorca’s classic, she remains the only actor to have won every official Best Actress prize currently awarded for a single UK theater performance. She wowed again in HBO Max’s I Hate Suzie, a brilliant panic attack of a dark comedy about a moderately famous actress thrown into turmoil when nude photos on her phone leak online.

For one reason or another, these projects didn’t land with as much force in the US as back home. Indeed, Piper co-created I Hate Suzie with her Effect playwright Lucy Prebble, and the show aired right after other stellar series from British female multihyphenates, like Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag and Michaela Coel’s I May Destroy You. Rest assured, Piper’s BAFTA-nominated performance is every bit as ferociously compelling — and revealing — as what her peers delivered in those Emmy-winning smashes.

For a good chunk of American audiences, at least, Suzie remains a hidden streaming gem waiting to be discovered. Piper seems comfortable in that zone.

Elsinore dramatizes the heartbreaking, inspiring final act of Ian Charleson, a gay actor not out publicly who was known for his starring role in Chariots of Fire. Charleson decided, shortly after being diagnosed with AIDS, to play Hamlet at the National Theatre while fighting for his life — and somehow pulled it off. Scott’s turn as the late great dominates the movie, but Piper becomes its sneaky heart. Patsy, Charleson’s best friend, emerges as his caretaker and as an anchor in their defiant chosen family.

“Their relationship was beautiful chaos,” Piper says. “They partied hard. He was a big figure in her daughter’s life. She was a single mother working in a male-dominated industry.” When it came to Charleson’s controversial choice to play Hamlet — his doctor, portrayed by Olivia Colman, was initially firmly against it — Patsy simply got it. So did Piper. “It makes complete sense to want to play one of, if not the most challenging parts at your most vulnerable point in your life as you approach your death,” Piper says. “Patsy understood that about him. I understand that about what he chose to do as well. I think a lot of actors get it, to be honest.”

Elsinore is a tearjerker, no doubt, but it’s stuffed with joy. Piper brings plenty of levity with her glamorous, haughty embodiment of an old showbusiness powerhouse. She is clearly having a ball. “I really miss people like Patsy in our industry — the larger-than-life characters — because everything’s so serious and there’s no money now,” Piper says. “It was fun to pull from the characters I knew in my early career. There were agents I had who were cut from a different cloth. It wasn’t all terribly kind, but it was unlike anybody I’d grown up with — the flamboyance, the drama, the quick shifts in tone and mood.”

Her chemistry with Scott is undeniable. The two veterans of the London theater scene previously worked together on Lena Dunham’s critically acclaimed Catherine Called Birdy, including a birthing scene for the ages. Like Piper, Scott is plenty decorated back home, but his frequent co-star finds him unusually playful to work with.

“With that skillset, you expect someone who’s a bit of a dick, but he’s not remotely a dick — he is warm, he is generous, he is informal. The work feels casual,” Piper says of Scott. “He takes it seriously, of course — he knows what he wants and knows what he likes — but it’s not the only thing that’s happening in his life, which I think is healthy.”

Piper can relate. She’s a mother of three and values the separation of the personal and professional. “I do my work, then I go home and am a parent — and so there’s no real processing of what I’ve done in the day, which is often really thrilling and rare and something I’d wanted to do since I was a child,” she says. Take, for instance, the job she’s just come back from: Wednesday season three. Piper grew up on Tim Burton and was now surrounded by his and his team’s singular designs. She got to act opposite the likes of Winona Ryder. And she was gone for nine months, a very long time. Too long, maybe.

“I haven’t worked on a nine-month shoot since Doctor Who, and I left that show for a reason,” she says. “The gratitude is there, but also it’s not without a cost.” Now, of course, she’s even further away, in the American south: “I’m doing a lot of being away. I feel terrible and also excited.”

Some viewers read into the whirring, control-obsessed anxiety of Piper’s I Hate Suzie tour-de-force as a thinly veiled commentary on her own struggles as an artist in the public eye. (Suzie’s career beginnings mirrored Piper’s to some degree.) The show was fiction, of course, but Piper’s guttural performance came from somewhere true.

“It’s really fun to play,” Piper says now, “but it’s just no way to live your life.”

The lesson took some learning. “I need things to be beyond good for me to take it seriously, to take myself seriously — it’s really got nothing to do with anyone else, but with insane levels of achievement,” Piper says. “It’s dysfunctional. I’ve been like that since I was a kid.” She believed the work should feel painful, that it should take everything out of her. She credits Yerma, which she performed in London and New York from 2016-2018 under the direction of Simon Stone — who so happens to be the director of Elsinore — with ushering in a new way forward in that regard.

“Simon completely changed my career for me — completely changed the way I looked at acting,” Piper says. “That’s a nice thing to have in a career that has been going on for a long time, to suddenly work with someone that completely rips up the rule book.”

Brick by brick, Piper is building a thrilling new chapter on that experience. Elsinore has proven a cozy fit. Not just as an awards-bound prestige movie offering her a meaty supporting role — also in the way it’s welcoming her into spaces she’s never even thought much of before. Her main goal this awards season? To hang out with Club Kid writer-director-star Jordan Firstman. “I’ve watched Rotting in the Sun about five times. It’s so funny and so free,” she says, referring to Sebastián Silva’s graphic meta comedy that starred Firstman as a vapid version of himself. “Now I just want to be his best mate.”

She’s written a film that she describes as “romantic horror,” which she’s planning to direct. (Her feature debut, Rare Beasts, premiered at Venice in 2019.) She knows it will be difficult to get off the ground. But she’s been feeling inspired by what she’s seeing. “It’s really useful going into a process of trying to get a film made that may never happen, may never see the light of day — it’s energized my passion,” she says.

Same goes for the students with whom she spent the previous afternoon.

“Even though we live in this difficult day and age, even though it might feel more compromised and frightening in terms of a career choice, they still want to pursue this,” Piper says. “There is still this appetite for the arts. I find it quite moving.”

Elsinore opens in limited North American theatrical release on November 20.

#738. Mastodon Fights Lawsuit From Late Guitarist Brent Hinds’ Estate: ‘The Truth Will Be Addressed in Due Course’

"Honoring Hinds's legacy does not require rewriting the agreements governing his business interests," write attorneys for the heavy metal band in a new court filing.

Mastodon has filed its first legal response to a lawsuit brought by the estate of its late guitarist Brent Hinds — and the heavy metal band is pointing out what it sees as key foundational errors in the case.

Surviving Mastodon members Brann Dailor, Bill Kelliher and Troy Sanders urged an Atlanta judge on Monday (Nov. 2) to dismiss some of the legal claims brought by Hinds’ father in September. The guitarist died in a motorcycle crash in August 2025, a few months after Mastodon announced he’d be ending his 25-year run with the band.

Hinds’ family is suing to cash out his 25% stake in the band’s operations, arguing that an $80,000 check they received after his death was far too low. But Mastodon’s Monday court filing, obtained and first reported by Billboard, disputes this characterization of the facts. The band members say the amount of money due to Hinds’ estate will be hammered out later but that first, they want the court to trim away certain claims that “fail as a matter of law.”

“His contributions to the band’s legacy are undeniable, and his death was a profound loss. None of that is in dispute,” reads the court filing. “But honoring Hinds’s legacy does not require rewriting the agreements governing his business interests or imposing obligations on his former bandmates that Georgia law does not recognize.”

Among the claims that Mastodon wants cut from the lawsuit are counts for breach of fiduciary duty and conversion (a legalese term for theft). The band members say that even if Hinds’ family is owed more money for his shares, this should be dealt with as a simple contract matter rather than twisted to allege some larger wrongdoing.

Mastodon also wants the judge to dismiss claims over the artwork for the band’s August 2026 album Marrow Deep, which debuted at No. 2 on Billboard’s Top Hard Rock Albums chart. Hinds’ estate alleges that the album cover featured the guitarist’s likeness without its permission, but Mastodon argues that the lawsuit uses a technically flawed legal claim to make that point.

“These distinctions matter,” write the band’s lawyers in the motion. “Defendants therefore seek dismissal only of those claims, or portions of claims, that lack a legal basis on the face of the complaint. The parties’ remaining factual and contractual disputes — and the truth — will be addressed in due course.”

Reps for Mastodon and the Hinds estate did not immediately return requests for comment on Tuesday (Nov. 3).

Hinds was 51 years old when he died in Atlanta last year. At the time, he had been in the middle of negotiating the terms of his exit from Mastodon, and no final paperwork had been signed. Hinds said the decision was not a mutual one: “They kicked me out,” he wrote in an Instagram comment a week before his death.

#737. “You Shall Not Pass”: Gandalf, Black Panther and Deadpool Take to the Streets of France

Costumed protesters say superhero and fantasy imagery brings joy and a message to a movement over poor school conditions and the cost of living — even as Paris police crack down on masks.

High-school students in France protesting for basic educational needs have been joined by hundreds of thousands of multi-generational protesters angry about the soaring cost of living. Throughout October, across three consecutive Saturdays of demonstrations, a trend quickly emerged: costumed superheroes, wizards and knights supporting the movement.

This theatrical strategy mirrors the pageantry of the French Revolution, where wearing classic Greek and Roman costumes represented political expression and defiance. Yet, the Paris Police Prefecture doesn’t want any “secret identities” at protests and announced before Saturday’s Halloween Protest that it would enforce a 2010 anti-mask law and issue fines. The Hollywood Reporter spoke with some of the disguised protesters to better understand the message behind their chosen costumes and what they think of the fines. Related Stories Movies Josh O'Connor Calls Bond Speculation "Incredibly Bizarre Pinch Me Moment" General News British Celebrity Loses Legal Bid to Prevent Publication of Identity and Sexual Misconduct Allegations

Many French students returned to stifling, overcrowded, teacherless classrooms (with no substitute teacher for weeks) as the deadly heatwaves in Europe extended far past their usual summer boundary. Leaking roofs, unsanitary bathrooms, rodents, overloaded class schedules, lack of heating in colder months and a failing higher education admissions system only compounded the issue. What’s more, these students aren’t happy to enter a job market where AI and automated tools threaten to render their future careers obsolete before they even begin.

Hippolyte Leibovici, 29, a filmmaker (Mother’s), who dresses as Gandalf from The Lord of the Rings to protest, explains: “This movement started because young students wanted better conditions at school. If President Macron corrected that, well, the protests would have ended right away. I could see that from the other side of the world; it seems terrifying how the French people are protesting — but what you are seeing is an exceedingly small part of the protest — we are talking about less than 1 percent of the protesters.”

The costume, he says, also opens doors with the movement’s youngest participants.

“Because of my costume, high school kids ask for selfies, and we talk. I ask them how school is going, what they are studying and what they want to do next year. Every high school student I have talked to is already very politicized, very well-educated and has dreams that can’t be achieved because of a faulty system.”

By mid-September, students began blocking high school entrances across France, and the movement quickly grew; by October 5, the student-led unions called for national action to reform the education system. By then, the police had been called in. What came next was violence. Life-altering injuries by police include a 15-year-old student who lost a hand to an exploding stun grenade, a 14-year-old with a fractured jaw and teeth and a 14-year-old girl’s near-strangulation, all reported by AP.

By Oct. 8, 6,600 students, mostly under 18, had been arrested.“We got used to police violence, people losing their hand or eye; it’s just a normal Saturday. We know that at the end of the protest, we will get tear-gassed,” explains Leibovici. Social media clips of him as Gandalf delivering the iconic line “You shall not pass!” to riot police deploying water cannons and tear gas conjure a good-versus-evil image online.

But why dress up in the first place? “I can see that it truly brings joy during this dark moment in France’s history, and it’s important for people to see the light at the end of the tunnel,” he says. “Humor and satire do not diminish the seriousness of the struggle.”

Luca Kraether, 28, and Thomas Honoré, 30, from Montpellier, France, who dress as knights for the protests, are business partners at Mardieval, an audiovisual and 3D creation company. “Protesting in armor is a way for us to create a strong, symbolic image to support the movement,” they explain. “A knight is a figure that naturally attracts attention, and we also want to break certain stereotypes. This imagery is sometimes co-opted by the far-right as an identity symbol. We want to show that this history and culture do not belong to any political faction — it’s our shared heritage.”

Kreezy, a 37-year-old personal trainer from the Paris region, dresses as Marvel’s Black Panther as an act of solidarity and leans into the superhero symbolism. “[Black Panther] represents the Black African community and protects his country and people with powers,” he says. “The Black Panther represents me the most — I bring peace, joy, humor and hope. To build a better world, we need better people to trust — and who better than a Superhero beloved by the people to fulfill that mission?”

Known to police for his social media antics, BaddyDeadpool, 29, is a content creator from Lyon, France, who often goes viral for giving roses to the police. He believes his Deadpool costume embodies freedom: “Free to think, say, and do whatever he wants — always within limits and respectful of others.” When asked about the protests and why he’s there, he explains, “I’m with the protesters, not for violence; it just brings more violence. Depriving people of their right to protest, tear-gassing people and using batons to beat them is not the right police response.”

Since 2010, strict public order laws have made concealing one’s face in public spaces illegal. Ahead of the Oct. 31 protest, the Paris Police Prefecture cited the law and expressly warned protesters not to conceal their faces. Violators faced a 150-euro ($168) fine for wearing masks, while anyone carrying replica weapons risked up to a 45,000-euro ($50,362) fine and three years in jail. The prefecture did not respond to requests for comment.

The threat of fines didn’t faze Kreezy: “When it comes to individuals with bad intentions looking to destroy and smash things during demonstrations, [the fines are] a good thing. But now there’s no longer any distinction made between peaceful and violent protesters. I wouldn’t call it an attempt to stifle the movement, but rather an effort to control the public.” Knights Kraether and Honoré agree. “We understand that it may be legitimate for security reasons. However, we also believe it can become a tool of repression if it is applied too strictly or disproportionately. Security is important, but it should never serve as a pretext to prevent citizens from protesting peacefully and expressing their convictions.”

At the Oct. 31 protest in Paris, THR observed and photographed BaddyDeadpool with the police, and no one asked him to remove his mask. After the protest, he told us: “Nothing happened — the police acted smart. They don’t think I’m a bad guy, I guess.”

Everyone THR spoke to credited the power of costumes as a storytelling mechanism. “If we can remind our peers in the film industry that an idea, a bit of audacity, and a lot of passion are enough to tell a story, then we’ve already accomplished something,” explain Knights Honoré and Kraether.

French students are officially back from fall break and already remobilizing by defying orders not to protest. Hundreds of students are marching daily and riot police are on the scene. France is bracing for a massive, nationwide strike on Thursday, Nov. 5, with major demonstrations planned in Paris, Montpellier, Lyon and Toulouse.

Asked whether Gandalf will return to the front line, Leibovici didn’t hesitate.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we all begin to absorb the bitter news of Patrick Stewart's death at the age of 86, a flood of personal tributes are pouring in, reflecting this global treasure's wonderful life lived with a dignity and bravado that few mortals possess.

We’re getting just a hint of what Patrick Stewart meant to those who worked with him or knew him throughout his stellar career. Whether on stage with the Royal Shakespeare Company, on TV as the dashing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and in Hollywood spectacles like 1984's "Dune," four "Star Trek" feature films, and the many "X-Men" movies in which he portrayed Professor Charles Xavier, Stewart was always the consummate professional. His final screen performance arrives on Dec. 18 with "Avengers: Doomsday" where he’ll present his Charles Xavier character once more.

"Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end," Ian McKellen wrote on Instagram of his "X-Men" co-star and friend. "You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love."

William Shatner, a fellow Enterprise captain, offered his profound sense of loss on Stewart's passing. The legends shared the screen in 1994's "Star Trek: Generations."

"What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor," Shatner posted on Facebook. "From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed."

Akiva Goldsman, co-creator of Paramount+'s "Star Trek: Picard" and "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," delivered a sorrowful message in the aftermath of Stewart's death

"Patrick was not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood," Goldsman wrote. "Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of 'Star Trek' without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more."

Stewart's "Star Trek: The Next Generation" family shared their grief and offered up poignant words to try to describe what effect he had on their lives and profession.

"There's no one on this planet that I have acted with or directed more often than my late great friend Patrick Stewart," revealed actor and director Jonathan Frakes, who co-starred for over 35 years with Stewart as Commander Will Riker, in a touching statement. "He will be with me forever. May he rest in Peace."

Finally, Marina Sirtis posted a teary-eyed video in which she explained how much of an impact Stewart had on her life during their time together on "The Next Generation" series and films, in which she portrayed Counselor Deanna Troi beside him.

"Patrick, I loved you with all my heart," she said on Instagram. "I know you're up there now, reunited with all those that you've loved. But to say that you'll be missed down here is probably the understatement of the century. It was an honor to work with Patrick. It was more than an honor; it was the privilege of my life to work with him."

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#735. Steve Ellis, Love Affair Singer, Dies at 76

The singer was best known for British pop-rock band's hit cover of "Everlasting Love."

Steve Ellis, the singer of British pop-rock band Love Affair, has died. He was 76.

The musician died following “complications from a chronic illness,” according to a statement shared on his official Facebook page.

“It’s with a heavy heart that we share the news of Steve’s passing,” the post read. “After complications from a chronic illness, Steve peacefully left the world on the evening of October 30, 2026, in the presence of his loved ones.”

A specific cause of death was not disclosed.

Songwriter and longtime friend David Courtney also confirmed Ellis’ death in a Facebook tribute. “I am sad to announce the passing of my long time friend Steve Ellis sho left us yesterday,” Courtney wrote. “My thoughts are with Val and the family.”

Ellis rose to fame as the frontman of Love Affair in the late 1960s, when the British group scored its biggest hit with a cover of “Everlasting Love.” Originally released in December 1967, the song topped the U.K. singles chart in 1968, spending two weeks at No. 1, according to the Official Charts Company.

Written by Buzz Cason and Mac Gayden, “Everlasting Love” was originally recorded by singer Robert Knight and released in 1967. Knight’s version reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100, while Love Affair’s recording did not chart in the United States.

Other Love Affair singles also reached the U.K. top 10, including “Rainbow Valley” (No. 5), “A Day Without Love” (No. 6) and “Bring on Back the Good Times” (No. 9).

Ellis began his professional music career at age 15, joining a North London band called the Soul Survivors in 1966. The group changed its name to Love Affair in 1967, according to his website.

Ellis left Love Affair in 1969 and went on to form his own band, Ellis, in 1972 alongside keyboardist Zoot Money and other musicians. The group released two albums, Riding on the Crest of a Slump (1972) and Why Not? (1973). He later joined rock band Widowmaker, which released its self-titled debut album in the mid-1970s.

After leaving Widowmaker, Ellis stepped away from the music industry and took a job working at the docks in England. His life took a dramatic turn in 1981 after a forklift accident severely injured his feet, beginning a lengthy period of surgeries and recovery that he recalled as being “in and out of hospital to mend [his] mashed feet,” according to his website.

Love Affair reunited under Ellis in 1991, with the singer leading his own touring group, Steve Ellis’ Love Affair, through 1998. He also continued recording solo material, releasing Best of Days in 2008, an album featuring contributions from Roger Daltrey and Paul Weller.

#734. Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms

Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected

Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin

Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect

Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter

This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.

That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."

A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.

The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).

Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.

"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.

There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.

But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.

Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.

A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.

The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.

"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.

The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."

The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.

He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."

German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.

This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.

Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.

Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.

He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.

"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.

He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."

Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.

Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.

Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."

The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.

The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.

Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.

"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."

The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.

"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.

The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.

Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."

The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.

Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."

"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.

That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."

Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.

However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.

The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.

Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.

"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.

The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.

"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.

The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.

Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.

The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.

The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.

Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.

"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."

Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.

Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.

The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.

Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.

"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."

Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.

"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.

The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.

They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.

Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

#733. Rebecca Gayheart Opens Up About Eric Dane’s Final Days: “Everything Shifted”

The wife of the 'Grey's Anatomy' star, who died in February, less than a year after announcing his ALS diagnosis, spoke about how she had "no idea that was it" when Dane made his last hospital trip.

Rebecca Gayheart is opening up about Eric Dane‘s final days timed to the release of the Grey’s Anatomy star’s posthumous memoir, My Book of Days.

Dane died in February, less than a year after announcing his ALS diagnosis.

The actress, who married Dane in 2004 before embarking upon a divorce in 2018 and having that dismissed in 2025, said it didn’t initially dawn on her that the Euphoria actor’s last trip to the hospital would mark the beginning of the end.

“He had gone to the hospital so many times before, and they would patch him up, so to speak, and he would come home,” Gayheart said in an interview with Maria Shriver, portions of which aired on Tuesday’s episode of NBC’s Today, with additional material posting on Today.com. “And he’d be OK. And we’d go back to the normal routine, which did change week by week.” Related Stories TV Savannah Guthrie "So Touched" by Allison Janney's Words About Mom Nancy Guthrie at Emmys TV Mariska Hargitay Reveals How She Decided to Host the Emmys

And that’s how she initially approached his last hospital trip.

“I said, ‘Listen, I’ll be back. I have a dinner. I’m going to this event.’ I had no idea that that was it, that that week was going to be our last week,” Gayheart said. “And nor did my daughters. It really took a few days for us to understand the gravity of what that last trip to the hospital meant.”

But after a few days at the hospital, things started to turn serious.

“I think it was like day three in the hospital where it shifted,” Gayheart said. “Everything shifted. Just the tone of when the doctors were talking to us, and some of the information we were given.”

Though Dane knew he was dying, Gayheart was surprised by how fast it happened.

“A lot of people will say, ‘Well, at least you knew, and you could have those last conversations,’” she said. “But we didn’t know, because there is no road map. No one can tell you what the journey looks like because it’s so different for every patient.

“He was becoming more alive mentally, but losing all of his physical abilities. And for the girls, that was really hard to watch as well. But overall, it’s a blur, because it was just so overwhelming.”

Still, the family went ahead with their sleepovers in Dane’s hospital room.

“The girls and I just camped out there with him, and we had our family sleepovers,” she said. “And we brought in those little candles that aren’t real candles. They have batteries. And we played his favorite music, and we tried to make it as nice as you can be in the hospital room.”

#732. Suno Says Jason Isbell Lawsuit Over Artist ‘Identities’ Must Be Dismissed: ‘Nothing Unlawful About That’

The AI music company has filed its first major response to the novel lawsuit, which accuses it of violating musicians' likeness rights.

Suno is asking a judge to throw out a lawsuit claiming the AI music firm stole the artistic identities of Jason Isbell and other stars, arguing there’s “nothing unlawful” about seeking to replicate the “vibe” of a particular artist.

Isbell sued in August, accusing Suno of allowing users to “conjure up a beloved musician’s identity” by entering their name as a prompt in its AI song generator. It was a novel case centered on an artist’s likeness rights, unlike earlier litigation against AI labs over the use of copyrighted music to train models.

But in Suno’s first major response on Tuesday (Nov. 3), its lawyers say there is “nothing unlawful” about merely using an artist’s name to describe music, any more than it’s illegal for a human artist to say “let’s go for something here with more of a Jason Isbell vibe.”

“When people describe styles of music, they often use artists’ names as shorthand for the genre they perform in,” Suno’s lawyers write in a motion obtained and first reported by Billboard. “This case turns on the premise that the law somehow condemns that universal practice. In reality it does not; the First Amendment would not allow it to.”

Suno’s motion, which asks the judge to dismiss the case immediately, argues that Isbell’s lawsuit attacks “ubiquitous methods of communicating ideas” and would hurt the “creative and cultural ecosystem” if allowed to proceed.

An attorney for Isbell did not immediately return a request for comment on Tuesday.

Isbell and other artists sued in August, accusing Suno of violating artists’ likeness rights (also known as publicity rights) by encoding their entire musical personas as tokens in its AI model. The case was filed as a class action, seeking to potentially represent “millions” of other artists: “The platform is built to identify musicians by name and generate identity-evocative output on command. This is its product.”

Suno was already facing a slew of lawsuits from major music companies, who claim the company violated their federal copyrights by ingesting millions of songs to train their models. The new case was different, accusing Suno of breaching state laws in New York, California, Tennessee and elsewhere that protect a person’s name, image and likeness from commercial exploitation.

Suno says it doesn’t actually allow users to prompt its AI model with specific artist names. When users do enter artist names, the platform says it translates that request into “descriptive musical characteristics,” which can then be used to direct the model to generate a song. A prompt of “Duran Duran,” for example, might get redirected into one of “New wave, Synth-pop, Pop rock.”

Isbell’s lawsuit claims those safeguards are faulty and can be duped by merely using spaces, such as Taylor Swift with “t a y l o r s w i f t” or Bad Bunny with “b a d b u n n y.” Even when a name is translated into musical styles, Isbell says the model clearly still exploits an artist’s identity: “Suno built and trained a model to index musicians by name. It encoded musicians’ identities into its AI model to create its commercial product without consent.”

But in Tuesday’s response, Suno says those accusations are legally deeply flawed. Simply using the name of a real person as a “shorthand to convey information about the genre that they want to create in,” Suno’s attorneys argue, is not the kind of thing that has historically violated state-law likeness rights.

“The law does not prevent people from using names to find or describe information, nor does it prevent building a tool capable of recognizing those references and acting on the information they supply,” Suno’s lawyers write, arguing that a ruling to the contrary would violate the First Amendment’s freedom of speech.

Even if likeness rights worked that way, Suno says the case would still be doomed by federal “preemption,” a legal doctrine that bars state-level claims that interfere with existing federal laws. Allowing artists to sue to assert their state-level likeness rights in such a way, Suno says, would overlap too much with federal copyright law’s existing protections for creative works.

“Congress made the considered policy choice not to confer intellectual property protection on an artistic style, precisely to allow subsequent creators to build on the prior works of a genre,” Suno says. “[This lawsuit] would create a shadow state law IP regime … fundamentally conflicting with the federal regime that has been in place for more than two centuries.”

#731. Broadway Box Office: Tom Hiddleston In ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Starts Off Strong

'Other Desert Cities' was the top earner in a down week for Broadway.

Much Ado About Nothing, starring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell, held its first preview performance last week and played to 100 percent capacity, with the second highest average ticket price on Broadway last week at $238.

The Jamie Lloyd revival, which transferred to Broadway from London, brought in $358,262 in that one performance, and if ticket prices hold, the play could be one of the industry’s highest weekly grossers. The play opens Nov. 19 at the Winter Garden Theatre.

Other Desert Cities was the week’s highest earner with $2.35 million and the week’s highest average ticket price of $301, which is the highest yet for the play starring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Allison Janney and Joe Keery.

Hamilton was the second highest earner with $2.31 million, followed by Harry Potter and the Cursed Child with $1.63 million, MJ with $1.61 million and The Lion King with $1.56 million. Billy Crystal’s solo show, 860, was the sixth highest-grossing, with $1.35 million, despite three heavily comped press performances.

A Few Good Men, starring Bradley Whitford and Tom Blyth, opened on Broadway last week and brought in close to $1.3 million, despite a fully comped opening night as well as several comped press tickets in the leadup. The play, which opened to mixed reviews, played to 100 percent capacity last week.

Despite the addition of a new show to the lineup, Broadway grosses were down 13 percent and attendance down 4 percent, as the industry competed with Halloween and the New York City Marathon.

New play Downstate saw a slight drop in attendance in its second week on Broadway, down to 87 percent from 94 percent as it expanded to eight performances from six. The play brought in $275,085, ahead of its Nov. 15 opening.

New musical Wanted also saw a drop in attendance, down to 82 percent from 93 percent, with grosses falling to $508,919. The musical is scheduled to open Nov. 8.

SpaceX celebrated Halloween with an early-morning launch from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base today (Oct. 31) at 12:04 a.m. EDT (0404 GMT; 9:04 p.m. on Oct. 30 local time), sending 27 of the company's Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO).

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the 18th flight for this particular booster, which is designated B1093. The record for a SpaceX first stage is 37, set this past August by the booster B1067.

The Falcon 9's upper stage did its job as well today, deploying the 27 Starlink satellites into LEO about 62 minutes after launch. They're joining more than 11,000 spacecraft in the Starlink megaconstellation, which is by far the largest satellite network ever assembled.

SDA-T1TL-B | SDA-T1TL-C | Transporter-16 | 14 Starlink missions

Today's launch was the 118th Falcon 9 flight of 2026 so far. More than 70% of these missions have been devoted to building out the Starlink network.

SpaceX has also launched its Falcon Heavy and Starship rockets three times apiece this year. Falcon Heavy is an operational vehicle, but Starship remains in the test-flight phase. The company is currently gearing up for another Starship launch, which is expected to take place sometime in November.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #729. Karol G Sweeps Latin Airplay’s Top 3 With ‘No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto’ Tracks

"Thank you to everyone who listens to these songs, makes them their own, and takes them to places we sometimes never even imagined."

Sr. Charts & Data Analyst (Latin & Billboard Español)

Karol G makes history becoming the first artist on Billboard’s 32-year-old Latin Airplay chart to hold Nos. 1, 2 and 3 simultaneously with songs from one album, on the chart dated Nov. 7. Further, she’s just the third act, and only woman, to hold the entire top three, following Bad Bunny and J Balvin, who both did it in 2019 — but not with songs from the same album.

“It brings me so much happiness to see how music continues to connect with people in this way,” Karol G shares with Billboard. “Having three songs occupy the top three spots on the Latin Airplay chart is something that thrills me and fills me with pride — but above all, it makes me feel deeply grateful.”

As “BbY WOW” is back on top of the overall Latin Airplay chart, Karol sweeps the top three. The track, with Judeline and rusowsky, returns to No. 1 for a third week, generating 11.1 million audience impressions in the United States during the Oct. 23-29 tracking week, up 29%, according to Luminate. All three songs come from her album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, released in August, which spent 11 weeks at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums.

“Karol is in a special moment where different songs are connecting with different audiences at the same time,” Jose Cedeño, EVP & GM of Interscope Capitol Miami, tells Billboard. “Each record has its own story and momentum, and our job is to support what fans and radio are responding to. We don’t see these songs as competing with each other. There’s real demand for all three, and seeing them at No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 on Latin Airplay speaks to that connection and the range of her music.”

“BbY WOW” trades places with “Ahí,” with Drake, which dips to No. 2 after one week in charge, with 8.3 million impressions, down 10%. Meanwhile, “Alguien Que Te Amaba,” climbs to a new No. 3 high, up 31% to 7.6 million impressions.

“Behind every song, there is a story, a great deal of hard work, and an incredible team that makes it possible for the music to reach so far,” says Karol. “Thank you to everyone who listens to these songs, makes them their own, and takes them to places we sometimes never even imagined.”

While Karol G goes 1-2-3 on Latin Airplay with songs from the same album, Bad Bunny and J Balvin tripled up atop the list for a week each in August and September 2019, respectively.

On the August 3, 2019-dated ranking, Benito was credited on all three top spots. Starting with “Callaita,” from his album Un Verano Sin Ti, the song surged 7-1 for his first and only week in charge. The No. 2 spot belonged to “Que Pretendes,” with J Balvin, from their collaborative album, OASIS. Standalone cut “Soltera,” with Lunay and Daddy Yankee, rounded out the top three at No. 3.

J Balvin took over the top three on the chart dated Sept. 28, 2019. “Que Pretendes,” with Benito, led at No. 1. “No Me Conoce,” from Jhayco’s album Famouz, also with Bunny, rose to No. 2, and “China,” the all-star collaboration by Anuel AA, Daddy Yankee, Karol G, Balvin and Ozuna, came in at No. 3.

Elsewhere, “BbY WOW” adds an 11th week at No. 1 on the multi-metric Hot Latin Songs chart — the second-longest command in 2026 (behind Bad Bunny’s 31-week reign this year — 72 overall — through “DtMF”).

#728. Can Germany revive its economy before the far-right AfD gains ground?

Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Can new growth sectors create jobs and ease voters' economic fears, thereby helping contain the far-right AfD?

Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.

While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.

The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.

Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.

These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."

Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.

Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.

The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.

He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.

Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.

US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.

"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.

In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.

"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.

The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.

The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.

"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.

"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.
